title: Agree on team conventions
summary: Use a shared formatter, lint rules, and review process.
explanation: Choose conventions that make the codebase consistent and easy to change. Automate routine formatting so reviews can focus on behavior, and revisit rules when the project needs change.

title: Test important behavior
summary: Cover the behavior that users and other modules depend on.
explanation: Use tests to check expected results, important failure paths, and regressions. Match the level of testing to the change: a small pure function and an integration boundary need different checks.
caveat: The source recommends tests for every new module. Test depth should reflect behavior and risk; a line-count target alone does not establish useful coverage.

title: Enable strict checking
summary: Start with strict mode and choose additional checks deliberately.
explanation: Set strict in tsconfig.json to enable the strict checking family. Add noImplicitReturns, noUnusedLocals, and casing checks when they suit the project. Existing projects can tighten checks in stages.
caveat: The source lists four strict options. The strict family has grown; check the compiler version rather than treating that list as complete. noImplicitReturns and noUnusedLocals are separate options.

title: Keep type checking useful
summary: Avoid unnecessary any; use inference and explicit types where they help.
explanation: Let TypeScript infer straightforward local values. Add annotations at boundaries or where they clarify a contract. For untrusted or unspecified inputs, use unknown and narrow it before use.
caveat: The source discourages inferred variable types. Type inference is an intended TypeScript feature; redundant annotations are not required for sound everyday code.

title: Describe fixed string choices
summary: Use a literal union when only a known set of strings is valid.
explanation: A union makes allowed values visible to callers and lets the compiler catch misspellings. Keep a plain string when the value is genuinely open-ended, such as user-entered text.
bad:
type Job = { status: string };
const job: Job = { status: "finshed" };

title: Name things by their purpose
summary: Choose names that explain the role of a value or function.
explanation: Use the language of the problem and keep names precise. A name should explain why the value exists without repeating the entire implementation or encoding a policy that may change.
bad:
const d = 30;
function chk(n: number) { return n >= d; }

title: Reuse type transformations
summary: Use built-in utility types for common changes to a type.
explanation: Partial, Pick, Omit, and Readonly express relationships between types without manually duplicating their properties. Keep the resulting types readable and tied to the domain.
caveat: Readonly is a compile-time restriction and is shallow. It does not freeze an object or recursively make nested values immutable.
bad:
type Profile = { name: string; email: string };
type ProfileUpdate = { name?: string; email?: string };

title: Use const and let
summary: Prefer const for bindings you will not reassign, and let when reassignment is needed.
explanation: Block-scoped declarations make a value’s lifetime easier to follow. A const binding cannot be reassigned, while the contents of an object referenced by that binding can still change.

title: Prefer strict equality
summary: Use === and !== for comparisons without implicit coercion.
explanation: Strict equality keeps comparisons easier to reason about because it does not convert unrelated operand types. If coercion is intentional, make the conversion visible and validate its result.

title: Use clear literal syntax
summary: Prefer literals to unnecessary constructor calls.
explanation: Object, array, string, number, and boolean literals communicate the value directly. Use constructors when they provide behavior you need, such as building a regular expression from a dynamic pattern.
bad:
const title = new String("Report");
const rows = new Array();
good:
const title = "Report";
const rows: string[] = [];

title: Keep state out of the global scope
summary: Use modules and explicit dependencies instead of shared global variables.
explanation: Global state can couple unrelated code and create collisions. Export only the values a module needs to expose, and pass dependencies into code that uses them.
caveat: The source describes classic scripts sharing a global scope. ES modules have their own module scope, but explicitly attaching state to globalThis still creates shared global state.
bad: globalThis.currentUser = { name: "Alex" };

title: Separate responsibilities
summary: Organize code around responsibilities with clear boundaries.
explanation: Keep rendering, data access, and domain logic understandable and independently changeable. Choose file and component boundaries that suit the framework and the code’s behavior.
caveat: The source treats mixing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript as dangerous. Colocation in a component is a valid design choice; responsibility boundaries matter more than separating file extensions.

title: Keep control flow easy to follow
summary: Use early returns and small helpers to reduce deep nesting.
explanation: Handle exceptional or empty cases near the start, then leave the main path clear. Extract a helper when it gives a meaningful name to a piece of behavior.

title: Keep functions focused
summary: Give each function one clear responsibility.
explanation: A focused function is easier to read, test, and reuse. Split a function when the extracted piece has a useful purpose or name, rather than to satisfy a fixed number of lines.
caveat: The source suggests functions of 5–10 lines. Treat that as a prompt to review complexity, not a universal limit.

title: Make function arguments clear
summary: Group related options when positional arguments become hard to understand.
explanation: A small options object can name each setting at the call site and make optional settings easier to add. Keep the object cohesive instead of hiding an unrelated collection of values behind one parameter.
caveat: The source recommends one or two parameters. Argument count is a readability signal, not a correctness rule.
bad:
function exportReport(format: string, name: string, archived: boolean) {}
exportReport("csv", "orders", false);

title: Avoid unclear boolean arguments
summary: Use a named option or separate operation when a boolean hides intent.
explanation: A call such as save(true) is hard to interpret. Name the choice at the call site, or split separate behaviors into separately named functions when that makes the API clearer.
sourceTitle: Do not use flags as function parameters
caveat: Boolean options can be appropriate for a genuine on/off setting. The issue is unclear meaning or unrelated behavior, not the boolean type itself.
bad:
function save(force: boolean) {}
save(true);
good:
function save(options: { overwrite: boolean }) {}
save({ overwrite: true });

title: Write comments that explain decisions
summary: Explain constraints and intent; remove redundant or stale comments.
explanation: Keep comments for information the code cannot express clearly, such as a protocol requirement or a deliberate tradeoff. Delete commented-out code and update comments when behavior changes.
sourceTitle: Comment as much as needed but not more
bad:
// Add one to attempts
attempts += 1;
good:
// The provider counts the initial request toward the retry limit.
const retriesLeft = Math.max(0, requestLimit - attempts);

title: Measure loop performance
summary: Choose readable iteration, then profile real bottlenecks.
explanation: Use for, for...of, or an array method according to the operation. When iteration matters to performance, compare complete workloads on the runtime you ship and include allocation and early-exit behavior.
sourceTitle: Use the fastest way to loop arrays
caveat: The source calls for the fastest loop and caching length. No loop form is universally fastest; engine, data shape, workload, and semantics affect results.

title: Use array methods for their purpose
summary: Use map, filter, find, and other methods when they describe the operation.
explanation: Choose map to transform items, filter to select items, and find to retrieve the first match. A loop may be clearer for early exits or complex control flow. Avoid creating an unused array just to run side effects.
bad:
const names: string[] = [];
users.map(user => { names.push(user.name); });
good:
const names = users.map(user => user.name);
const activeUsers = users.filter(user => user.active);

title: Validate data at boundaries
summary: Check external data at runtime before trusting its shape.
explanation: Treat network responses, form submissions, stored values, and URL parameters as untrusted inputs. Use a schema validator or a focused type guard. A type assertion only changes compiler assumptions; it does not inspect a value.

title: Use consistent, clear blocks
summary: Keep control flow formatting predictable.
explanation: Use braces and a formatter to make branch boundaries obvious. Agree on semicolon and one-line conventions as a team, then automate them instead of revisiting them in each review.
caveat: JavaScript supports automatic semicolon insertion. The source’s blanket criticism of omitted semicolons is a style opinion; consistency and syntax awareness are what matter.

title: Use meaningful parameter defaults
summary: Provide a default when omitting an argument has a sensible meaning.
explanation: A default value documents normal behavior and reduces repeated fallback code. Leave an argument required when a guessed value would hide a caller error. Defaults apply to undefined, not to null or every falsy value.

title: Use spread and destructuring clearly
summary: Unpack values and copy structures when it improves readability.
explanation: Destructuring can name the properties a function needs. Spread can combine arrays and object properties without modifying the original container. Keep the operation simple enough that its result is apparent.
caveat: Array and object spread create shallow copies. Nested objects remain shared, and only iterable values can be spread into an array or function argument list.
bad:
const nextSettings = settings;
nextSettings.theme = "dark";
good:
const nextSettings = { ...settings, theme: "dark" };
const { theme, language } = nextSettings;

title: Use template literals for interpolation
summary: Build strings with visible interpolation when it is clearer than concatenation.
explanation: Template literals keep embedded expressions near the text they belong to and support multiline strings. They do not escape HTML, SQL, or shell syntax; use the destination’s safe encoding or parameterization.
bad: const label = name + " has " + count + " tasks";
good: const label = `${name} has ${count} tasks`;

title: Handle unexpected switch inputs
summary: Choose an explicit fallback or an exhaustive type check.
explanation: A switch over open input should account for unexpected values. A switch over a closed union can use never to make a newly added case fail at compile time instead of silently taking a fallback.
caveat: A default that silently returns a normal result can conceal missing union cases. Match the fallback to the domain and error behavior.

title: Name booleans as questions
summary: Use names such as isReady, hasAccess, or canEdit when they fit the meaning.
explanation: A boolean name should make the true and false cases easy to read in a condition. Favor positive names when a double negative would obscure the branch.
sourceTitle: Use the prefix "is" and "has" for Booleans
bad:
const access = user.role === "editor";
if (access) openEditor();
good:
const canEdit = user.role === "editor";
if (canEdit) openEditor();

title: Declare values near where they are used
summary: Keep declarations close to their purpose and within the smallest useful scope.
explanation: Grouping a value with the work that uses it reduces the distance a reader needs to search. Initialize it when meaningful, and lift a declaration only when its scope or lifecycle requires that.
caveat: The source recommends putting declarations at the top of every function. With block-scoped const and let, declaring near use is often clearer; this is an editorial update to the original advice.

title: Initialize values deliberately
summary: Give a variable a useful starting value when it is declared.
explanation: Prefer creating a fully usable value over declaring a variable and assigning it much later. If absence is a real state, model it with an optional or union type rather than a misleading placeholder.
caveat: Do not invent empty strings, zeroes, or empty objects solely to avoid an uninitialized variable. Those values may have valid domain meanings.
good:
const title = "Report";
const selectedId: string | undefined = undefined;

title: Use iterators for streamed sequences
summary: Use a generator when values can be produced on demand.
explanation: An iterator exposes one value at a time and works with for...of. A generator can express that process without materializing a complete collection. Use an async generator when producing each item requires asynchronous work.

title: Keep calculations pure where practical
summary: Make calculations depend on inputs and return results without changing outside state.
explanation: Separate calculation from effects such as network requests, logging, and persistence. Pure calculations are straightforward to test because the result does not depend on hidden mutable state.
caveat: Purity does not imply idempotence. A pure function that adds one is deterministic, but applying it twice changes the result twice.

title: Prefer predictable state updates
summary: Avoid mutating shared values when a new value makes changes clearer.
explanation: Immutable updates can make ownership and change detection easier to understand. Use readonly types to express intent, and copy only the parts that must change. Local mutation can still be appropriate when it is contained and clear.
caveat: Immutability is not an automatic performance improvement. Copying has a cost, and readonly types do not enforce runtime or deep immutability.

title: Keep side effects explicit
summary: Make state changes and external operations easy to locate.
explanation: Keep effects at clear boundaries and avoid surprising changes to shared inputs. Explicit dependencies make code easier to test and help readers see where network, storage, and user-interface work occurs.
caveat: Useful programs need effects. The goal is to control and name them, not remove every effect.

title: Name meaningful constants
summary: Replace unexplained domain values with names that describe their purpose.
explanation: A named constant documents the rule and gives maintainers a single place to update it. Keep obvious arithmetic values inline when a name would add noise rather than meaning.
bad: const expiresAt = createdAt + 86400000;
good:
const millisecondsPerDay = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
const expiresAt = createdAt + millisecondsPerDay;

title: Simplify repeated branching
summary: Use clear conditions, lookup tables, or polymorphism when they fit the problem.
explanation: Keep a straightforward if statement when it expresses the rule well. Consider a lookup table or separate implementation when repeated branching makes related behavior hard to maintain.
caveat: The source presents avoiding conditionals as a general goal. A conditional does not by itself mean a function has too many responsibilities.

title: Handle errors at useful boundaries
summary: Throw Error objects and decide where failures can be recovered or reported.
explanation: Keep useful context when propagating failures. Treat caught values as unknown and narrow them before reading properties. Avoid swallowing errors or returning a success-shaped value when an operation failed.

title: Use promises for asynchronous results
summary: Use promises and async/await to make asynchronous flow clear.
explanation: Await operations when their results are needed and handle rejections. Use Promise.all for independent work when appropriate. Keep callback-based APIs when they model repeated events rather than a single eventual result.
caveat: The source says callbacks are synchronous and promises speed up code. Callbacks can be synchronous or asynchronous. Promises describe eventual results; they do not make CPU work parallel or inherently faster.

title: Avoid unnecessary dynamic behavior
summary: Prefer explicit code over eval, string timers, and changes to built-in prototypes.
explanation: Dynamic code evaluation and changes to built-in behavior make programs harder to inspect and can introduce security or compatibility problems. Use ordinary functions and well-defined module APIs.
sourceTitle: Do not use weird JavaScript features
caveat: The source groups several language features together. Using array length or the void operator can be intentional and valid; evaluate the specific behavior instead of banning every listed feature.
bad: setTimeout("refreshReport()", 1000);
good: setTimeout(refreshReport, 1000);

title: Build against web standards
summary: Use supported web APIs and feature detection for browser differences.
explanation: Check for the capability you need rather than identifying a browser by its name. Use progressive enhancement or a suitable fallback when a feature is unavailable to the people using the site.
sourceTitle: Do not yield to web browser whims

title: Avoid unnecessary parser-blocking scripts
summary: Choose module, defer, or async according to the script’s dependencies.
explanation: Module scripts defer by default. Classic external scripts with defer run after parsing, in document order; async scripts run when ready. Use async only when execution order is independent.
sourceTitle: Place scripts at the bottom of the page
caveat: The source recommends putting every script before the closing body tag. Modern loading attributes and module scripts offer more precise control; moving a script is not the only solution.
bad:
<head>
  <script src="report.js"></script>
</head>
good:
<head>
  <script type="module" src="report.js"></script>
</head>

title: Batch expensive DOM work
summary: Avoid repeated layout work in hot paths.
explanation: Keep DOM reads and writes organized and update only what changed. Profile rendering when it affects responsiveness. Use safe DOM construction or framework rendering rather than inserting untrusted HTML strings.
sourceTitle: Keep DOM access to a minimum
caveat: Not every DOM access is expensive. Layout-triggering reads mixed with writes deserve attention; the source’s string-to-DOM suggestion must not become unsafe HTML insertion.

title: Separate changeable settings from logic
summary: Keep configuration and translated text easy to find and override.
explanation: Use clear configuration types and an explicit source of values. Separate user-visible messages from application logic when the product supports translation. Validate configuration at its boundary.
caveat: Public client configuration must not contain secrets. Put credentials and private service keys on the server.

title: Start with useful HTML behavior
summary: Use native controls and links so core interactions have a solid baseline.
explanation: A link should remain a real link, and a form should expose clear fields and submission behavior. Add JavaScript to improve the experience while keeping accessibility and failure paths in view.
bad: Guides
good: Guides

title: Measure before replacing a library
summary: Use native APIs when they meet the need; compare performance using the real workload.
explanation: A dependency can add download, initialization, and runtime costs, but it may also implement useful optimizations or remove substantial maintenance work. Compare the complete behavior, bundle impact, and measured bottleneck before replacing it.
caveat: The original heading makes an absolute claim. Native JavaScript is not universally faster than every library implementation. TypeScript type checking also does not run in the browser; compare the emitted JavaScript and actual workload.
bad:
// Assumption: every library call must be replaced to be fast.
// No profile or equivalent-behavior comparison has been made.

title: Keep imports useful and organized
summary: Remove unused imports and group dependencies consistently.
explanation: Imports should make the module’s dependencies easy to scan. Use the editor, formatter, or current lint tooling to keep them tidy, and use import type when a dependency is needed only for types.
caveat: The source links to TSLint rules. TSLint is legacy tooling; use the tools supported by the current project. Preserve imports whose purpose is an intentional side effect.
bad:
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
export const load = readFile;
good:
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
export const load = readFile;

title: Organize code into clear modules
summary: Group related behavior and expose a small, intentional API.
explanation: A module should make a responsibility easy to find and change. Extract shared behavior when it has a stable purpose, and avoid adding layers that merely forward a call without clarifying ownership.

title: Load optional code when it is needed
summary: Use logical code-splitting boundaries to reduce initial work.
explanation: Dynamically import an expensive feature when the user requests it, or prefetch it when the need is predictable. Provide a loading state and handle import failures so the feature does not appear unresponsive.
caveat: Too many tiny splits add request and coordination overhead. Do not delay code that is necessary for the first useful view.

title: Compress transferred assets
summary: Use HTTP compression for text assets when the hosting platform supports it.
explanation: Brotli or gzip can reduce transferred JavaScript, CSS, and HTML bytes. Verify the deployed response headers and transferred size instead of assuming a build artifact is compressed in transit.
caveat: Savings depend on the asset and compression settings. Compression reduces transfer size; it does not directly reduce the JavaScript work the browser executes.

title: Minify production assets
summary: Use the production build to remove unnecessary source characters and optimize output.
explanation: Let the build tool handle minification rather than manually shortening source code. Keep source maps according to the project’s debugging and disclosure needs, and check the resulting bundle size.
caveat: Minification and HTTP compression are different steps. Compression should still be configured at the serving layer.

title: Use Lighthouse as one quality check
summary: Audit the deployed page and investigate the findings that affect users.
explanation: Lighthouse can identify performance, accessibility, and other web quality issues in a controlled run. Combine it with manual interaction checks and, when available, real-user measurements.
caveat: A score is a diagnostic signal. Run conditions and tool versions affect it, and an automated accessibility audit does not cover every accessibility requirement.

title: Move suitable CPU work off the main thread
summary: Use a worker when a heavy calculation would block interaction.
explanation: A worker runs JavaScript in a separate execution context and communicates through messages. Keep the input and output contract clear, handle worker errors, and clean up workers when the work is finished.
caveat: Workers cannot directly access the DOM. Startup, message transfer, and serialization have costs, so a worker is not automatically faster for small tasks.

title: Use primitive type names
summary: Use string, number, boolean, and symbol instead of their boxed type names.
explanation: Boxed object types describe wrapper objects and rarely match what an API intends to accept. Use object for a non-primitive value, or a more specific object shape when its properties are known.
sourceTitle: Number, String, Boolean, Symbol and Object
scope: Declaration files and general type annotations
caveat: object means non-primitive. It is not a replacement for unknown when the input may be a primitive, and it does not describe a specific property shape.
bad: declare function normalize(value: String): String;
good: declare function normalize(value: string): string;

title: Make generic parameters meaningful
summary: A generic parameter should participate in the type relationship.
explanation: Use the parameter in members, arguments, or results so the type carries information. If the parameter has no role, remove it or model the relationship that the API actually needs.
scope: Declaration files and generic API design

title: Use unknown for unspecified inputs
summary: Keep an unknown value checked until its type has been established.
explanation: Any disables checking through subsequent uses. Unknown accepts an unspecified value but requires narrowing before reading properties or calling it. Keep unavoidable any at a deliberate, documented boundary during migration.
scope: Declaration files and general type annotations
caveat: The handbook specifically allows any as a migration aid. Unknown still requires runtime validation when external data must match a particular shape.

title: Use void for ignored callback results
summary: Declare a callback result as void when the caller does not use it.
explanation: Void expresses that the API discards the returned value and prevents the implementation from treating that value as unchecked data. It describes how the result is used, rather than forbidding the callback from returning a value.
bad: declare function onReady(callback: () => any): void;
good: declare function onReady(callback: () => void): void;

title: Make callback parameters optional only when they can be absent
summary: Describe the arguments the API actually supplies to the callback.
explanation: A callback parameter marked optional means the callback may be invoked without that argument. Callers can already supply a callback that ignores extra arguments, so optionality is not needed just to let a callback accept fewer parameters.
caveat: Use an optional callback parameter when the API really can omit that argument. The example assumes elapsedMs is always supplied.

title: Avoid overloads that only change callback arity
summary: Use one callback signature with the arguments the API provides.
explanation: A callback can ignore arguments, so separate signatures for a zero-argument callback and a one-argument callback are usually redundant. The shorter overload can also admit callbacks that should have been checked against the fuller contract.
bad:
declare function beforeTask(action: () => void): void;
declare function beforeTask(action: (done: () => void) => void): void;

title: Put specific overloads first
summary: Place narrower call signatures before general fallback signatures.
explanation: TypeScript resolves calls using matching overload signatures, so an early broad signature can hide a later specific case. Order signatures so the intended return type is selected for specific inputs.

title: Replace trailing-argument overloads with optional parameters
summary: Collapse equivalent signatures when their return type is the same.
explanation: If the only difference is the presence of trailing arguments, a single signature with optional parameters is usually clearer. Preserve required relationships between arguments and keep separate signatures when their behavior or return types differ.
caveat: The handbook’s rule applies when all collapsed overloads have the same return type. Making an earlier parameter optional must not accidentally permit an unsupported argument combination.
bad:
declare function compare(left: string): number;
declare function compare(left: string, right: string): number;
good: declare function compare(left: string, right?: string): number;

title: Use unions for equivalent overload inputs
summary: Combine one-position input alternatives when they share the same result contract.
explanation: A union parameter lets callers pass a value that is already a union. Keep an overload when a different input shape determines a different return type or enforces an important argument relationship.
caveat: Do not make the parameter optional if the zero-argument form returns a different type. The handbook deliberately keeps that signature separate.
